en.title: Daily routine
en.goal: Describe everyday activities and tell the time.

phrases.t: I get up at seven o'clock every day.

dialogue.title: Asking about routine
lines: What time do you get up every day?
I get up at 7 and go to work at 8 every day.
What time do you get off work today?

dian-hours.title: Telling time with 点
dian-hours.body: To tell the time in Chinese, the number is followed by 点 (diǎn), which works like "o'clock". It is a simple, direct structure: number + 点.

fuso-horario-unico.title: All of China uses the same time
fuso-horario-unico.body: Although China's territory is wide enough to span 5 geographic time zones, the whole country uses a single official time: Beijing time (北京时间). This means that in the far west of the country the sun can rise much later on the clock than in the east — but everyone tells the time the same way.
examples: Beijing time (the official time for the whole country)

time-before-verb.title: Time words before the verb
time-before-verb.body: Unlike English, where "every day" can go at the end of the sentence, in Chinese time expressions always come before the verb, usually right after the subject.
examples: I get up at 7 every day

zai-progressive.title: (正)在 + verb — an action in progress
zai-progressive.body: To say that an action is happening right now, Chinese uses 在 (zài) or 正在 (zhèngzài) before the verb — it works like English "to be + -ing".

zai-progressive.title: "Měitiān" or "xiànzài"?
zai-progressive.body: Měitiān (每天, every day) marks a habit. Xiànzài (现在, now) marks the present moment, often used with this zài of action in progress — different from the "zài" of location that you will see in the next unit.
examples: I get up at 7 every day (habit)
what time is it now? (present moment)

review.why: 点 is 'o'clock' in time expressions; 'hour(s)' as the PT gloss
